title: Terror-Free Turkey Bill Reaches Parliament, F-16s Deploy to Estonia for NATO, Akkuyu Nears Commissioning
subhead: The government-backed PKK disarmament legislation enters parliament this week with a 15-article draft and a verification mechanism, as Turkey deploys five F-16s to Estonia for NATO air policing. Rosatom says Akkuyu's first reactor is months from commissioning, UN chief Guterres begins the first Cyprus visit in 16 years, and the US hits Turkey with 12.5% tariffs under a new forced-labor regime.

sections.heading: Terror-Free Turkey Bill Heads to Parliament With Verification Mechanism
sections.body:
The government-backed 'terror-free Turkiye' initiative enters a decisive legislative phase this week, with a 15-article draft bill expected to be submitted to parliament establishing the legal framework for PKK disarmament and dissolution, according to Hurriyet Daily News.

Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus held consultations with representatives from the AKP, MHP, DEM Party, CHP, and the New Path bloc on the bill's outlines. The legislation is expected to be a joint initiative by at least three parties — the AKP, DEM Party, and MHP — and will be discussed by the Justice Commission on July 29 or 30 before a General Assembly vote targeted for July 31, ahead of the summer recess.

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on July 25 that the proposal does not include a general or individual amnesty but contains provisions concerning PKK members. The law's implementation would be conditional on verification of PKK disarmament, with a special monitoring mechanism drawing on field reports from MIT and the Turkish Armed Forces. Two DEM Party lawmakers met with jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan on July 20 at Imrali prison island, and DEM Party co-chairs are scheduled to visit political parties next week.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first concrete legislative step after months of back-channel talks. If passed, it creates a legal path for PKK disarmament — but the verification condition and absence of amnesty mean the process will be contested by both hardline nationalists and Kurdish activists demanding broader concessions.

sections.heading: Turkey Deploys F-16s to Estonia for NATO Air Policing
sections.body:
Turkey will deploy five F-16 fighter jets and 76 personnel from the 181st Panther Squadron based in Diyarbakir to Amari Air Base in Estonia for NATO's Baltic air policing mission, running from August through November, Hurriyet Daily News reported.

The deployment underscores Turkey's continued commitment to NATO's eastern flank even as the alliance navigates internal tensions over the Iran war, spending targets, and Turkey's own defense procurement disputes. Turkey has periodically contributed to Baltic air policing since 2006, but this rotation comes at a moment when Ankara is simultaneously pushing for F-35 reentry and negotiating S-400 transfer conditions with Washington.

The Diyarbakir-based squadron's assignment to the Baltics also carries symbolic weight — the same airbase is central to Turkey's domestic counter-PKK operations, and rotating its assets to a NATO mission signals that alliance commitments remain a priority despite competing demands.
sections.whyItMatters: The F-16 deployment is a calibrated signal: Turkey remains invested in NATO's collective defense even while pressing its own defense procurement agenda. It also puts Turkish pilots in direct proximity to the Baltic front line with Russia at a moment when Russian airspace violations are rising.

sections.heading: Akkuyu Nuclear Plant Enters Final Pre-Start Phase, Rosatom Says
sections.body:
Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said on July 24 that commissioning work at Turkiye's first nuclear power plant is 'only months away,' signaling that the long-delayed project is entering its final phase before the first reactor begins commercial operations.

The announcement followed a meeting in Moscow between Likhachev and Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, who said the two countries discussed the strategic importance of their energy partnership, including progress at the Akkuyu plant in Mersin province. The project consists of four VVER-1200 reactors with 4,800 MW combined capacity, expected to generate roughly 10% of Turkiye's electricity once fully operational.

Construction of the first reactor has faced delays from supply-chain disruptions, sanctions-related obstacles, and financing issues. Rosatom and Turkish officials have said the first unit is expected to begin operations before the end of 2026, with the remaining three units scheduled through 2028.
sections.whyItMatters: If Rosatom's timeline holds, Akkuyu's first reactor coming online would mark Turkey's entry into nuclear power — a structural shift in a country that imports nearly all its energy. The timing matters: with Hormuz disruption driving oil above $100, domestic nuclear generation gains added economic and strategic urgency.

sections.heading: Guterres Begins First UN Chief Visit to Cyprus in 16 Years
sections.body:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres arrives in Cyprus on July 27 for a three-day visit — the first by a sitting UN secretary-general in 16 and a half years, since Ban Ki-moon's trip in early 2010, Hurriyet Daily News reported.

Guterres is expected to hold separate meetings with Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhurman and Greek Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides before bringing the two leaders together for a joint meeting. He will also meet members of the island's bicommunal technical committees and civil society organizations.

According to Greek Cypriot media, the UN is considering two paths: convening another informal 5+1 conference before the end of Guterres's term if conditions allow, or continuing engagement at the UN General Assembly in September before handing the portfolio to his successor. A separate report says the UN is weighing a 'strategic agreement' that would reaffirm the bizonal, bicommunal federation parameters and establish a two-year negotiation timetable, including measures to facilitate international flights through Ercan Airport and strengthen Turkish Cypriot trade under the Green Line Regulation.
sections.whyItMatters: Guterres is making a late-term push on Cyprus before his mandate expires at year's end. The visit itself signals that the UN sees a narrow window — but whether it produces anything beyond atmospherics depends on whether both sides are willing to move beyond long-entrenched positions on sovereignty and governance.

sections.heading: US Slaps 12.5% Tariffs on Turkey Under Forced-Labor Regime
sections.body:
The United States imposed new tariffs on 60 trading partners on July 24 under a forced-labor framework, replacing an expiring global duty rolled out by President Trump earlier this year. Turkey was placed in the higher 12.5% tariff bracket, alongside China, Japan, South Korea, and dozens of other economies deemed insufficient on forced-labor import prohibitions, according to Hurriyet Daily News citing the US Trade Representative.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the targeted economies represent the majority of US trade. The EU, Canada, India, and the UK received the lower 10% rate because they have implemented or committed to forced-labor import bans.

The measures followed a months-long investigation and are considered more resistant to legal challenges than earlier Trump tariff actions struck down by the Supreme Court in February. Goods already facing sector-specific tariffs, like steel and aluminum, are exempt, as are certain energy products and fertilizers. Turkey's textile and agricultural exports — key sectors that reached $2.35 billion in fresh produce alone in the first half of 2026 — face higher costs in the US market under the new regime.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's placement in the 12.5% bracket — rather than the 10% rate given to EU members and others with forced-labor laws — reflects Washington's assessment that Ankara hasn't done enough on labor standards. At a time when Turkey is trying to deepen economic ties with the US after the NATO summit, this tariff layer compounds the cost of doing business.

sections.heading: Ozel's New Party Names Leadership Team as CHP Collapses to 44 Seats
sections.body:
New Party leader Ozgur Ozel appointed a 10-member executive board on July 25, retaining several allies from his CHP tenure. Ensar Aytekin will oversee party organizations, Nurhayat Altaca Kayisoglu overseas groups, and Zeynel Emre continues as spokesperson. Yunus Emre was named secretary-general.

The move formalizes the split that saw 91 lawmakers — including Ozel — resign from the CHP on July 24 to establish the New Party, which immediately became the second-largest bloc in the 600-seat parliament after the AKP's 277 seats. The rump CHP fell to 44 seats, dropping behind the DEM Party (56) and the MHP (46).

The split traces to a May court ruling that annulled the CHP's 2023 leadership election, removed Ozel as chairman, and reinstated Kemal Kilicdaroglu. Ozel's appeal to the Court of Cassation was not taken up before the judicial recess. Kilicdaroglu said the CHP had 'largely completed its purification,' referencing ongoing investigations into CHP-run municipalities. Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu remains imprisoned on graft charges since March 2025. The New Party reportedly will not initially seek transfers from CHP mayors to avoid destabilizing local administrations.
sections.whyItMatters: The opposition landscape is now formally fragmented. With the New Party at 91 seats and the rump CHP at 44, the AKP's 277-seat bloc faces two opposition centers instead of one. Whether that weakens or clarifies the challenge to Erdogan depends on whether the two opposition blocs can coordinate — or whether they cannibalize each other's voter base ahead of 2028.

sections.heading: Turkey Condemns West Bank Settler Violence as Israel Expands Operations
sections.body:
Turkey's Foreign Ministry condemned escalating settler violence in the occupied Palestinian territories after four Palestinians were killed during a confrontation involving Israeli settlers, troops, and residents near the West Bank city of Nablus on July 24.

The ministry said the four were killed by 'settler terrorists encouraged by the Netanyahu government,' describing the incident as 'a consequence of Israel's ongoing genocidal policy.' It called on the international community to ensure accountability for attacks and land seizure.

Following the Nablus-area violence, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz ordered expanded military operations, additional troop deployments, and new checkpoints across the West Bank. They also called for faster authorization of settlement outposts. Far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich called for Palestinian villages to be treated like Beit Hanoun in Gaza and for the army to act with an 'iron fist.' Settlers subsequently attacked several Palestinian villages near Nablus, setting fire to homes and property, according to Palestinian officials. The Palestinian Health Ministry said 87 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank this year.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's condemnation is consistent with its long-standing position, but the West Bank escalation — settlement expansion orders, ministerial calls for collective punishment — adds pressure on Ankara at a time when it is also mediating in the Iran conflict and managing its own Kurdish peace process domestically.

bottomLine: A consequential Sunday for Turkey's domestic and strategic agendas: the terror-free Turkey bill enters parliament with a concrete 15-article framework and verification mechanism, giving the Kurdish peace process its first legislative shape. Ozel's New Party formalized its leadership with 91 lawmakers, confirming the opposition's permanent split. On the external front, Turkey sends F-16s to Estonia for NATO duty, Rosatom signals Akkuyu is months from commissioning, and the US places Turkey in the 12.5% tariff bracket. Guterres's arrival in Cyprus — the first UN chief visit in 16 years — could open a narrow diplomatic window, but expectations should remain modest. Meanwhile, US-Iran de-escalation talks mediated by Pakistan and Qatar remain fragile, and Turkey's condemnation of West Bank settler violence adds another layer to its already crowded diplomatic portfolio.
sources: Hurriyet Daily News, Anadolu Agency, AP, Reuters, Milliyet, UN, Al Jazeera
